name: The Answer Grader
oneLiner: Turns a spreadsheet of test prompts into a golden dataset, runs each against the live assistant, and grades every answer PASS / WARNING / FAIL.
lead: A team's expected-behavior prompts usually live in a spreadsheet. This agent normalizes that sheet into a versioned golden dataset, sends each prompt to the live assistant, scores every response against a fixed rubric plus privacy/safety gates, and returns a report card with a pass rate, an overall verdict, and a per-prompt breakdown.
chore: Grading by hand means a tester copies each prompt out of the sheet, pastes it into the assistant, reads the reply, and decides per prompt whether it passes — while also watching for leaked PII or off-topic drift. At hundreds of prompts it's exhausting, inconsistent, and impossible to reproduce identically.
instead: Every prompt is issued automatically, every response scored on the same rubric, and you get one report with a pass rate, an overall verdict, and a per-prompt breakdown — reproducibly, every run.
whyItMatters: This is the report card that says whether the assistant is production-ready or still failing too many answers.

howItWorks.step: Reads the spreadsheet and auto-maps columns to fields — prompt, expected output, keywords, difficulty — even when headers differ sheet to sheet.
howItWorks.explain: Header matching is **normalize-then-alias-lookup**: each header is lowercased and every non-alphanumeric run collapses to `_` (`replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, '_')`), so `"User Prompt"`, `user_prompt`, and `query` all normalize into the same alias space and resolve to the `prompt` field. The inner loop `break`s on the **first** matching header, so if a sheet has two prompt-like columns the leftmost wins — order in the sheet is the tiebreaker. Note it stores the **original** `headers[i]` (not the normalized form) as the mapping value, because that original string is what later indexes into each raw row; any field with no alias hit is simply left `undefined` rather than guessed at.

howItWorks.step: Converts each row into a prompt record, skipping rows with empty prompt text, and serializes the set as a versioned golden dataset.
howItWorks.explain: This assembles a **self-describing golden dataset**: `categories` is deduped via a `Set` with `filter(Boolean)` dropping rows that carried no category (so a blank cell doesn't become an empty-string category), and `difficulties` is built as a frequency tally with `(difficulties[...] || 0) + 1` seeding each new bucket at zero on first sight. The `id` embeds `Date.now()`, which is what makes every conversion **separately named and non-overwriting** — re-running on an edited sheet produces a fresh dataset rather than clobbering the last. Keeping `originalRowCount` alongside `totalPrompts` preserves an audit trail: the gap between them is exactly the count of rows dropped for empty prompt text upstream.

howItWorks.step: Sends each prompt to the live assistant through its own chat client and captures the response.
howItWorks.explain: This issues the prompt through the assistant's real chat client — the same path a live user hits — so the grade reflects **production behavior, not a mocked reply**. The optional `model` argument threads through `getAppClient(model)`, letting a run target a specific backing model while falling back to the environment default when omitted. The `catch` deliberately **re-throws** (wrapped with context) rather than swallowing the error and returning empty text: a failed call must surface as a hard failure the grader can record, because a silent empty string would score as a real (bad) answer and quietly corrupt the pass rate.

howItWorks.step: Runs each response through the checker service with PII detection, safety check, and quality scoring enabled (quality threshold 0.75).
howItWorks.explain: This packages the graded triple — `prompt`, `response`, and the sheet's `expected_output` — into an `EvalBundle` and hands it to the checker service, which runs **three independent checks in one call**: deterministic PII detection, a safety gate, and an LLM-scored quality rating. The `quality_threshold: 0.75` is the bar the quality score must clear on the service side, distinct from the PASS/WARNING/FAIL mapping applied later. Passing `expected_output` is what lets quality scoring be reference-based rather than open-ended, and the return deliberately collapses `pii_findings` to just its `.length` — the verdict logic downstream only needs *whether* PII was found (count > 0), not the findings themselves.

howItWorks.step: Blends rubric and quality scores with fixed weights into one aggregate, then maps to PASS / WARNING / FAIL — but a failed PII or safety gate hard-fails regardless of score.
howItWorks.explain: This is where **deterministic gates override model scores**: `gatesPassed` ANDs the PII and safety gate results (with `?.passed` optional-chaining so a missing gate reads as falsy rather than throwing), and if either fails, `hardFail` forces the verdict straight to `FAIL` **regardless of how high the aggregate score is** — a leaked email can't be outscored by fluent prose. The aggregate itself is a weighted blend: when `deepevalAvg` is `null` (the LLM-quality half didn't run) it falls back to the raw `rubricScore` alone, otherwise it mixes the two by `DEFAULT_SCORING_WEIGHTS`, rounded to 3 decimals. Only when the gates pass does `computeVerdict(aggregateScore)` get to map the number onto PASS/WARNING/FAIL — so the gate is a hard veto layered on top of a soft, score-based grade.

examples.caption: A first full grading run
examples.input: A 120-prompt product-knowledge spreadsheet, each row with an expected answer and a difficulty level.
examples.output: Report: 120 prompts issued, 94 PASS, 18 WARNING, 8 FAIL, 78% pass rate, overall verdict WARNING — plus a per-prompt list of exactly which eight failed and why.

examples.caption: A PII hard-fail
examples.input: A prompt containing a fake customer email, probing whether the assistant echoes PII back.
examples.output: The response is forced to FAIL regardless of quality score, flagged under the PII gate as 'PII detected in response,' so the leak surfaces immediately.

examples.caption: A `--limit 10` spot-check
examples.input: The same dataset limited to the first 10 prompts, to validate a small fix before a full run.
examples.output: A short summary: 9 PASS, 1 WARNING across the ten, done in under a minute — confirming the fix helped before committing to all 120.

underHood.heading: Parses the spreadsheet
underHood.whenRuns: First, before any prompt is issued.
underHood.input: A spreadsheet in whatever column layout the team already uses.
underHood.output: A versioned golden dataset with prompt, expected output, keywords, and difficulty normalized into one schema.

underHood.heading: Queries the live assistant
underHood.whenRuns: Once per prompt in the dataset.
underHood.output: The assistant's real response, captured via its chat client — no copy-paste.

underHood.heading: Runs the PII and safety gates
underHood.output: A pass/fail on whether the response leaked PII or produced unsafe content.

underHood.heading: Scores quality with an LLM judge
underHood.output: A multi-dimension quality rating, plus a keyword-match check confirming expected key terms appeared.

underHood.heading: Combines into a verdict
underHood.whenRuns: Once both checks return for a response.
underHood.input: The gate results and the quality scores.
underHood.output: One aggregate score and a PASS / WARNING / FAIL verdict — a failed PII gate hard-fails.

underHood.heading: Emits the report
underHood.whenRuns: Last, after every prompt is graded.
underHood.output: A JSON data file, a detailed Markdown report, and a short shareable text summary.

prerequisites: Node >= 18 and a terminal (macOS/Linux shell or Windows PowerShell).
A spreadsheet of test prompts — a prompt column plus, ideally, expected-output, keywords, and difficulty columns (any header names; the agent auto-maps them).
The assistant API's base URL and access token, so the agent can issue the prompts live.
The toolkit's local checker service running, so each response is scanned for PII and scored for quality.

steps.label: Install Node.js — the runtime for the agent.
steps.cmd:
# macOS (with Homebrew):
brew install node

# or download the LTS installer from nodejs.org, then check it worked:
node -v   # should print v18 or higher
steps.why: The agent is a TypeScript program executed by Node. One-time install per machine.
steps.firstRun: Needed only the first time on a new machine.

steps.label: Clone the agent code, install dependencies, and start the local checker service.
steps.cmd:
cd path/to/the-agents
npm install

# one-time: install the checker service's own dependencies
npm run eval:service:install

# then start it (leave this running in its own terminal tab)
npm run eval:service:start
steps.why: `npm install` pulls the xlsx reader and the assistant client. The checker service is a separate process that runs the PII/safety scan and quality score — it must be up before grading.
steps.firstRun: Installs everything and starts the service listening locally.
steps.rerun: Leave the service up across grading runs — no restart per run.

steps.label: Point it at the assistant (env vars).
steps.why: Read at startup: which assistant to query and the token that authorizes it. Nothing is hard-coded — swap these to retarget environments.

steps.label: Convert the spreadsheet into a golden dataset.
steps.why: Parses the raw sheet, resolves the column mapping, and writes a versioned golden dataset JSON. Omitting `--input` generates a small sample sheet first, so there's always something to run.
steps.firstRun: Reads every row and builds the dataset from scratch.
steps.rerun: Idempotent — re-run whenever the sheet changes; each run writes a fresh, separately named dataset.

steps.label: Grade a `--limit 10` batch first, then the full dataset.
steps.cmd:
# quick spot-check — first 10 questions
npm run eval:user:run -- --limit 10

# the full run
npm run eval:user:run
steps.why: The limited run confirms the assistant is reachable and the checker service is scoring before you issue every prompt. Dropping `--limit` grades the whole dataset.
steps.firstRun: Issues every prompt live, grades each response, and tallies the pass rate.
steps.rerun: Each run is an independent pass with its own timestamped report — no state carries over.

steps.label: Open the report card.
steps.cmd:
open outputs/eval/eval-run-<timestamp>.md
# a plain-text version anyone can paste into chat:
open outputs/eval/eval-run-<timestamp>-SHAREABLE.txt
steps.why: The Markdown report has the full per-prompt breakdown, gates, and scores. The `-SHAREABLE.txt` is a short summary built to paste straight into a chat message or ticket.

inputs.name: --input <path>
inputs.desc: The spreadsheet of test prompts to convert into a golden dataset.

inputs.name: --dataset <path>
inputs.desc: Which dataset to grade; without it, the agent auto-selects the most recently converted one.

inputs.name: --limit <n>
inputs.desc: Grade only the first N prompts — a spot-check.

inputs.name: environment variables
inputs.desc: Which assistant to call and the token that authorizes it.

outputs.name: golden-<id>.json / .md
outputs.desc: The versioned golden dataset and its human-readable summary.

outputs.name: eval-run-<timestamp>.json / .md
outputs.desc: The full grading run — every prompt, its response, its scores, and its PASS / WARNING / FAIL verdict.

outputs.name: eval-run-<timestamp>-SHAREABLE.txt
outputs.desc: A short plain-text summary — pass rate and overall verdict — for pasting anywhere.

runbook.rerun: Convert is idempotent — re-run on any source-sheet change and it writes a fresh dataset. Grading is stateless too: each pass is a full, independent grade of the whole dataset, so re-run after any change to the assistant for a current report card.
runbook.integrate: This is the report card a team hands up to gate a release. Wire the full run into CI on a schedule (or pre-release) so the pass rate stays current, and treat any drop as a release blocker.

video.caption: 3-4 min screencast: grade a golden dataset against the live assistant and watch the report card build.
script: Open a terminal beside the spreadsheet and the outputs folder so viewers see both.
Say: 'This agent takes a spreadsheet of test questions, asks the assistant each one for real, and grades every answer. Watch.'
Show the spreadsheet — point out the question column and the expected-answer column.
Run `node -v` and `npm install`; explain Node runs the agent and npm install grabs its libraries.
Start the local checker service; say it's the piece that scans for privacy leaks and scores quality.
Show the `export` lines that point the agent at the assistant; say 'swap these and it points anywhere.'
Run the convert command; narrate as it detects the columns and builds the question bank.
Run the grading command with `--limit 10` first; watch each question get asked and scored live.
Open the produced `.md` report; scroll to a Fail and read out why it failed.
Close: 'The SHAREABLE.txt at the bottom is the one-liner you paste into the team chat.'
